diagrams.title: Thevenin & Norton at a port — and maximum power
diagrams.cap: Any linear network seen from two terminals is a source V<sub>TH</sub> in series with R<sub>TH</sub> (or I<sub>N</sub> in parallel with R<sub>N</sub> = R<sub>TH</sub>). V<sub>TH</sub> is the open-circuit voltage, I<sub>N</sub> the short-circuit current, R<sub>TH</sub> their ratio; an ideal voltage source across the port makes R<sub>TH</sub> zero. Maximum power is drawn when R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>TH</sub>.
diagrams.qq: Voc = 24 V, Isc = 2 A. RTH and Pmax?

diagrams.title: Ideal sources and linear elements: what is allowed
diagrams.cap: Two ideal voltage sources may be in parallel only if they are equal (KVL), and two ideal current sources may share a loop only if they set the same current (KCL); a voltage source with a current source is always allowed. R, L and C are linear because their defining relations are straight lines through the origin; a diode is nonlinear.
diagrams.qq: Can a 5 V and a 10 V ideal source be put in parallel?

diagrams.title: Node and mesh analysis — set up any circuit
diagrams.cap: Node analysis writes Kirchhoff's current law at every node except the reference; mesh analysis writes Kirchhoff's voltage law round every window. A voltage source between two nodes becomes a supernode; a current source shared by two meshes becomes a supermesh. The number of independent meshes is b − n + 1.

diagrams.title: Network toolkit: dividers, source conversion, star–delta
diagrams.cap: Voltage divides in proportion to resistance and current in inverse proportion. A practical voltage source V in series with R behaves exactly like a current source V/R in parallel with R. A star of three resistors can replace a delta (and back) with the product-over-sum formulas; equal arms give R<sub>Y</sub> = R_Δ/3.
diagrams.qq: Delta of three 9 Ω resistors → star?

diagrams.title: Cells in series and parallel, with a balanced bridge
diagrams.cap: Series cells add their EMFs (a reversed cell subtracts) and their internal resistances; equal cells in parallel keep the EMF and divide the resistance. A bridge whose arm ratios match carries no current in its middle arm, so it reduces to two series pairs in parallel.
diagrams.qq: Four cells of 2 V, 0.5 Ω in series, one reversed. EMF and r?

diagrams.title: Resistance vs temperature
diagrams.cap: R<sub>T</sub> = R₀[1 + α(T − T₀)] for metals. Alloys with α ≈ 0 are used for standard resistors and shunts.

formulas.name: Nullator, norator & nullor
f: compare — open circuit : V = anything, I = 0
notes: Where: V = voltage across, I = current through the element
Tip: Open circuit: V anything, I = 0 · Short circuit: V = 0, I anything · Nullator: V = 0, I = 0 · Norator: V and I both anything.

formulas.name: Millman's theorem & neutral shift
notes: Where: E<sub>k</sub> = source emf in branch k (V), Z<sub>k</sub> = branch impedance (Ω), V<sub>n</sub>′n = star-point shift (V)
Tip: Parallel sources with series R: convert to Norton and add currents.
Example: 10 V / 2 Ω, 20 V / 4 Ω and 0 V / 4 Ω in parallel: V = (5 + 5 + 0)/(0.5 + 0.25 + 0.25) = 10 V.
TNPSC / ESE / APGENCO PYQ: TNPSC PG Q96

formulas.name: Ohm's law
notes: Where: V = voltage (V), I = current (A), R = resistance (Ω)
Tip: Triangle: V on top, I and R below — cover the one you want: V = I × R, I = V ÷ R, R = V ÷ I.
Example: LED on 12 V: drop 2 V at 20 mA → R = 10/0.02 = 500 Ω (use the next value, 560 Ω).
TNPSC / ESE / APGENCO PYQ: TNPSC 04/26 Q151

formulas.name: Power
notes: Where: P in watt
Tip: Triangle: P on top, V and I below. Series (same I) → I²R. Parallel (same V) → V²/R.
Example: 2 kW, 230 V heater: I ≈ 8.7 A, R = 26.45 Ω. On 200 V the same R gives 200²/26.45 ≈ 1512 W (P ∝ V²).
TNPSC / ESE / APGENCO PYQ: ESE 2026 Q101

formulas.name: Energy & charge
f: one chain : E = QV = VIt = Pt
notes: Where: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 1 unit
Tip: Triangle: E on top, Q and V below. Relationship map: Q = It → E = QV → E = VIt → E = Pt (P = VI). TNEB 2018 Q57: 10 A × 240 s = 2400 C.

formulas.name: Voltage divider
notes: Where: V<sub>s</sub> = supply voltage (V), R₁, R₂ = series resistors (Ω), V₂ = voltage across R₂
Tip: Same resistor on top.
Example: 24 V across 4 kΩ + 8 kΩ: V across 8 kΩ = 24 × 8/12 = 16 V. Loading it with another 8 kΩ makes the lower arm 4 kΩ → 12 V.

formulas.name: Current divider
notes: Where: I<sub>s</sub> = total current (A) entering two parallel branches R₁, R₂ (Ω); I₁ = current in R₁
Tip: OTHER resistor on top.
Example: 6 A into 2 Ω ∥ 4 Ω: I(2 Ω) = 6 × 4/6 = 4 A, I(4 Ω) = 2 A — the smaller resistor takes more.

formulas.name: KCL and KVL
notes: Where: I = branch currents (A), V = voltage rises and drops (V)
Tip: KCL → charge conservation; KVL → energy conservation. Link to energy: Q = It, E = QV = VIt = Pt.
Example: 12 V battery, 2 Ω in series with (6 Ω ∥ 3 Ω): R = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω, I = 3 A. KVL: 3 × 2 = 6 V + 6 V across the pair = 12 V
✓. KCL: 6 Ω takes 1 A, 3 Ω takes 2 A → 1 + 2 = 3 A ✓.

formulas.name: Thevenin & Norton
f: R<sub>th</sub> = resistance seen with sources killed
notes: Where: R<sub>th</sub> = resistance on the source side (seen from the load terminals); R<sub>L</sub> = resistance of the load
Tip: Kill sources: voltage source → short, current source → open. Maximum power when R<sub>th</sub> = R<sub>L</sub> (next row).
Example: 24 V source with 4 Ω in series and 12 Ω across the terminals: Vth = 24 × 12/16 = 18 V, Rth = 4 ∥ 12 = 3 Ω, IN = 6 A. RL = 6 Ω → IL = 18/9 = 2 A.

formulas.name: Tellegen's theorem
f: Σ v<sub>k</sub> i<sub>k</sub> = 0 over all branches
(v and i taken with associated reference directions)
notes: Where: v<sub>k</sub>, i<sub>k</sub> = voltage (V) and current (A) of branch k
Tip: Needs only KCL and KVL, so it holds for linear, non-linear and time-varying networks. It is the network form of conservation of power: power delivered = power absorbed.
